articles.title: Ukraine says Starlink connection 'now stable' after network limits
articles.snippet: The slowed Starlink connections had affected the Ukraine's military and drone operations for a week.
articles.full_text:
Ukraine says Starlink connection 'now stable' after network limits
- Published
Ukraine now has a "stable connection" to Starlink, its defence minister has said, after its military suffered days of restricted connectivity on the satellite internet network.
Kyiv relies on the Starlink and its military-grade counterpart Starshield for piloting drones and operations within Ukraine, but last week accused US President Donald Trump of telling owner Elon Musk to place limits on it.
This meant drones would lose connection when travelling at 161km/h (100mph) or more, it said. Trump denied doing so before saying Musk had "put it back".
Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said that speeds of more than 400km/h were now possible on the network, indicating that full capability had been restored.
"This result is above all important for our front, for our soldiers, for the operation of drones, for logistics and for communications," he said in a statement on Saturday.
Ukraine's military uses the network of 10,000 low Earth orbit satellites extensively for military operations, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield.
Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, which Musk said was controlled by the US military when he suggested the Pentagon could be behind the recent issues.
Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.
The debacle over Starlink began last week, and emerged during a broader diplomatic row between Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.
Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move criticised by Ukraine and its European allies.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.
While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war.
Zelensky said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied.
Meanwhile, fighting on the ground continues.
Russia's ministry of defence wrote on Telegram on Saturday that their air defences shot down 616 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones, striking a number of regions across the country, including Russian-annexed Crimea.
Sergey Aksyonov, the region's Moscow-backed governor, said restrictions on electricity and water had been put in place because of power cuts caused by the drone strike.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian authorities said they struck a missile component manufacturer, a chemical plant and an aircraft at a military airfield inside Russia in the past 24 hours.
They also said that Russia carried out 88 air strikes using 309 glide bombs and 10,270 kamikaze drones on Friday.

articles.title: Arrest made after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat
articles.snippet: Some 200 emergency personnel were deployed to fight the blaze at the Nazi dictator's Alpine residence in Germany.
articles.full_text:
Arrest made after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat
- Published
Police in the southern German state of Bavaria have detained a 33-year-old German man during a fire at Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, the Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest.
Dispatchers in Traunstein received a fire alarm from the building at 21:15 local time (19:15 GMT) on Friday and firefighters found it engulfed in flames. No injuries were reported, while difficult terrain hindered efforts to extinguish the blaze.
Police said they apprehended the suspect riding a motorcycle near the scene and told reporters that any possible motive was still being examined.
Some 200 emergency personnel were deployed and a criminal investigation has been launched.
Local police official Gerhart Holzinger told a press conference there was currently no evidence of any further suspects.
The residence, above the town of Berchtesgaden, was one of several buildings in the area used by the Nazi dictator and his entourage during World War Two.
Hitler and top Nazi officials used his nearby Berghof residence to plan the invasion of the USSR in 1941 and the whole complex was considered one of his headquarters.
He also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature.
Local media reported that site had been "largely destroyed", with the public urged to avoid the area.
Bavaria's Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann told reporters that the site would "under no circumstances remain a ruin", broadcaster BR24 reported.
"It is important that we continue our work of remembrance," he said.
Completed by the Nazis in 1938, the Eagle's Nest, which sits at an elevation of around 1,800m (5,900ft), escaped destruction after their defeat in 1945.
Since then, it has become a popular tourist destination and houses a mountain inn.
It serves as "a cautionary reminder of the abysses of the inhumane Nazi dictatorship", according to its official website, external.
During WW2, Hitler and his followers were responsible for the deaths of tens of millions of people, including the mass murder of European Jews. Homosexuals, gypsies, the disabled and ethnic minorities were sent to concentration camps and put to death.
There has been a wider debate in Germany and Vienna over whether to preserve, repurpose or demolish buildings connected to Hitler.
While some say these buildings should be preserved for historical reasons, others have raised concerns that they could be used as monuments or places of pilgrimage for neo-Nazis and far-right extremists.
In June, Berlin authorities announced they would tear down one of Hitler's bunkers - described at the time as "the power centre of Nazi Germany" - to build flats and offices on the site.
Those critical of the plans said the bunker had "significant historical value" and that it should have been turned into a museum and memorial site with an exhibit about the end of the war.
And in July, after years of controversy, Austrian authorities refurbished the house in the town of Braunau am Inn in which Hitler was born and turned it into a police station.

articles.title: Father who killed Oregon school gunman describes anguish over children he couldn't save
articles.snippet: Kaylub Giamanco has been hailed as a hero for killing a teenager who fatally shot three children and a teacher.
articles.full_text:
Father who killed Oregon school gunman describes anguish over children he couldn't save
- Published
A father who fatally shot a gunman at his daughters' school in the US state of Oregon has described his anguish over being unable to save more pupils after "hearing children pleading for their lives".
Three students and a teacher were killed by a 16-year-old former student at Silver Rail Elementary School earlier this month. The attacker was then killed by Kaylub Giamanco.
"I want to apologise for not saving their babies," Giamanco, who has been hailed as a hero, said of his thoughts for the parents of the children killed, in an interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting (OPB) that aired on Friday.
"The gratitude for saving people's children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn't save."
Giamanco, 36, said he wanted to meet the victims' families and "cry with them and hold them".
He credited a teacher who fought the attacker with giving him the chance to intervene without losing his own life.
"I would love to give her a hug because that's a real true hero," he said.
The students who were killed were all boys, aged five, eight and 11. They were among six people in total who were shot in a classroom at the school, police said. Alongside the teacher who was killed, another child and a teacher were wounded.
Giamanco told OPB that the day of the attack began with breakfast and making packed lunches. He and his wife had spent extra time getting their daughters ready because it was school picture day.
The carpenter had taken lunch to work but decided to go home to eat with his wife instead. That decision brought him past the school as the attack began.
He initially wondered whether someone carrying a long gun was playing a prank. Then he saw him fire at a pickup truck and head towards the school.
Giamanco retrieved a handgun from his vehicle and called emergency services.
"I said, 'I'm sorry, I have to go in. People are going to die'," he told the broadcaster.
He followed the attacker, who shot through the school's locked glass doors. Hearing children pleading for their lives and more gunfire, Giamanco crawled towards the building.
"I told myself this is probably the last thing that I'm ever going to do," he said.
Giamanco crawled through a shattered window and reached the classroom, where a teacher was locked in a struggle with the gunman. He opened the door and fired.
Giamanco told OPB he fired again when the attacker reached for his weapon. He then placed his own gun on the ground and raised his hands as an officer appeared.
He described feeling like the "last line of defence" between the children and the gunman, and said he "was supposed to be there" that day.
Afterwards, he called his wife to say he would not be home for lunch and that she needed to get to the school immediately. He then called his mother to tell her what had happened.
"Mum, I just had to take the life of what I think is might be a child because he ran into my daughter's school with a gun," he said.
Police identified the gunman as Griffin J John II - a former pupil who had attended special education classes at the school. His motive remains under investigation.
Police said the teacher who confronted the attacker had thrown her phone at him, tackled him and fought to take his shotgun. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said she "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed".
The youngest victim was Rhoam Summer, aged five. His father said the family was "broken and lost".
Megan Lambert, 25, the teacher who was killed, was working in what her family described as her "dream job".
"She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs," they said.
The other two boys have not been publicly named at their families' request.
The injured teacher has been named as Becky Drury, 54. She said in a statement shared with US media that the gunman shot her as she tried to shut her classroom door.
Giamanco's name became public less than a day after the shooting. His mother, Kenda Freeman, read a family statement saying he was not seeking recognition and asking for privacy.
Shortly after the attack, Oregon Governor Tina Kotek praised his intervention while acknowledging its emotional cost.
"Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well," she said.
Giamanco told OPB he now lies awake after his family goes to bed, replaying the attack.
"I relive, I see faces, I hear voices, I hear screams."

articles.title: British woman dies after trying to rescue sons swept away at sea in the Bahamas
articles.snippet: The children were subsequently rescued from the water, police say.
articles.full_text:
Mum dies after trying to rescue sons swept away at sea
- Published
A woman has died after attempting to rescue her two sons when they were swept away while snorkelling in the Bahamas.
The Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers on the island of Bimini launched an investigation into the sudden death of a 36-year-old British woman on Tuesday.
The force said it believed the woman - thought to be from Stapleford in Nottinghamshire - had been snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
In an attempt to rescue her sons, "the woman was also swept away", police said. The children were subsequently rescued from the water.
Foul play 'not suspected'
In a statement, posted on social media, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said: "According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town police station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini Ferry Dock.
"Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life.
"Preliminary information indicates that the deceased was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
"In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept away.
"She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered.
"Foul play is not suspected at this time.
"An autopsy will be conducted to assist in determining the exact cause of death."
A spokesperson for the Foreign Office added: "Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.
"We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family."

articles.title: Student movement takes Serbia's Vučić to the wire in neck-and-neck election
articles.snippet: The Student List has emerged from almost two years of anti-corruption protests to form the biggest challenge to Vučić's rule.
articles.full_text:
Student movement takes Serbia's VuÄiÄ to the wire in neck-and-neck election
- Published
If Sunday's parliamentary elections really are a battle for the heart of Serbia, then who better than a cardiologist to be one of the leading figures in the race.
Ilija SrdanoviÄ appears an unlikely opponent for Serbia's long-serving leader, Aleksandar VuÄiÄ, arriving for an interview by motorbike sporting a fluorescent yellow jacket emblazoned with pro-student slogans.
He has been selected as top candidate for an opposition movement posing the most serious challenge to VuÄiÄ since the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) entered government in 2012.
The Student List has emerged from almost two years of anti-corruption protests led by young Serbians, outraged by the deaths of 16 people when a railway station's canopy collapsed in Serbia's second city Novi Sad.
What you need to know about Serbia's pivotal election
- Published1 day ago
Instead of running for office themselves, student-led assemblies at the country's university faculties have chosen 250 candidates to stand in the parliamentary election, with SrdanoviÄ, professor at Novi Sad University, heading the list.
"It is absolutely normal to stand with my students to help them in their fair struggle," SrdanoviÄ told the BBC.
The Student List is up against a Serbian leader who has served successively as deputy prime minister, prime minister and president since 2012. When he called these snap elections last month, he stood down as president to run again for the role of prime minister.
Whatever VuÄiÄ's title, there has never been any doubt that he was the man in charge â an image enthusiastically promoted by Serbia's largely uncritical media.
He retains strong support among a significant section of Serbia's population. They view him as a strong leader who stands up for the country's interests. He can also point to significant economic growth over the past decade and numerous improvements in infrastructure.
VuÄiÄ has painted the student movement as foreign-backed and seeking to "bring down our state". "Let us always protect and defend it," he told supporters at a final campaign rally.
Just like the protest movement from which it developed, the Student List has no hierarchy or nominated leader. This makes it a proposition unlike any other in Serbia's relatively short democratic history.
Reliable polls are thin on the ground, but analysts are predicting an extremely tight vote.
Ilija SrdanoviÄ may head the list of candidates â but he is not the movement's leader and would not necessarily be first choice prime minister if they won.
SrdanoviÄ insists that the Student List has a clear vision: "We offer to our citizens the core values of civilised society, which this previous regime has taken away from our citizens for the last time."
The other candidates on the Student List range from academics to athletes â and economists to engineers. None of them has a political background. But the students who selected them believe that is a strength, rather than a weakness.
"We've gathered people who are actually the best in their fields, and we really think that they are competent enough to rule the country," says Aleksandra, a student at Novi Sad University who only wants to give her first name.
"All of them are gathered around the same vision of a country where the freedom of speech is ruling, where you can walk to your home in the middle of the night and you will not be beaten up by some hooligans," she adds.
The Student List and its supporters say that Aleksandar VuÄiÄ and the SNS dominate state institutions and media coverage.
At the last parliamentary election in 2023, the International Election Observation Mission noted "overwhelming ruling party advantage" due to "bias in the media" and "misuse of public office and resources".
The BBC approached leading figures in the SNS for an interview but was not offered a response.
For the past 18 months, there has also been a full-time, pro-SNS camp in the small park between the National Assembly and the Presidency building in the centre of Belgrade. Its residents have repeatedly attacked journalists and made the park a no-go zone for local people.
VuÄiÄ has called the camp "a symbol of resistance" against those who "cannot stand different opinions".
But his major challenge remains what happened outside Novi Sad railway station two years ago.
The station's renovation was a key part of his signature infrastructure project â the high-speed line linking Belgrade and Budapest. So it has been difficult for VuÄiÄ to distance himself from the disaster.
Protests followed, with participants accusing the authorities of corruption and having "blood on their hands".
"This is a problem for the government," says Magda Anastasijevic, the Eastern Europe analyst for the conflict monitor, ACLED.
"VuÄiÄ has survived this in the past, he was always able to find a scapegoat and blame whatever problems on them. This was not the case for the canopy."
On the diplomatic front, he has performed a delicate balancing act.
Membership talks with the EU continue, albeit fitfully, even as Serbia retains close ties with Russia and China â both countries that refuse to recognise Kosovo's unilateral declaration of independence from Serbia.
VuÄiÄ has warned those links could be severed if the Student List took power.
"When you ask them: will you impose sanctions on Russia? Silence, umming and ah-ing, but no answer," he told the audience at a pre-election rally.
"You know what the Chinese think, you've heard what Vladimir Putin said. So you decide. Think about who has our best interests at heart."
The final rallies of the campaign saw the SNS stage an event at Belgrade Arena, with Aleksandar VuÄiÄ as the only speaker. But on the other side of the Sava River, the Student List attracted a reported 150,000 people in Slavija Square to listen to a mixture of students and candidates.
The contrasting visions were clear to see: the strong, sole leader â or a collective approach. Now Serbia's electorate must decide which they prefer.

articles.title: Woman, 65, becomes second patient to die of Ebola in Kenya
articles.snippet: She was a close family member of the first victim, a man who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo.
articles.full_text:
Woman, 65, becomes second patient to die of Ebola in Kenya
- Published
Kenya has recorded its second death from Ebola as it handles its first ever outbreak of the disease.
A woman, aged 65, who was a close family member of the first victim, a man who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, died after being placed in quarantine, the health ministry said.
Seven other Ebola patients were receiving treatment at two isolation facilities, it added.
All the cases were within "one cluster, with no evidence of community spread", the ministry said.
More than 4,000 people have died in Africa since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease.
Kenya's latest victim had been under quarantine when she developed symptoms on 13 October, the health ministry said.
The first death, on 5 October, was that of a man who fell ill in September and was treated in several hospitals in DR Congo before arriving in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, where he died a few days later.
Those still being treated are three other relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner.
The US has warned its citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are also on alert.
Ebola is a rare but deadly disease, external caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The Bundibugyo species of Ebola is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
With more than 9,500 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread.
Kenya has introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from DR Congo and nine other countries it considers to be at high risk: Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.
Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights and present a QR code to port health officials on arrival.
Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases.
Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital.
Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed?
- Published3 days ago
Woman with Ebola in Nigeria confirmed as wife of Swiss diplomat
- Published1 day ago
Nigeria's health minister said its sole confirmed case of Ebola appeared to be genetically related to a strain identified earlier in Kenya.
Prof Ali Pate said there was no evidence so far that the Kenyan patient had travelled to Nigeria, but that further testing was under way.
Health officials have been investigating whether Nigeria's first case crossed paths with Kenya's first patient. Both are believed to have travelled through Uganda's Entebbe airport earlier this month.
Uganda's health ministry announced on Friday that people who had travelled to DR Congo would no longer be able to transit via Uganda as part of its prevention measures.

articles.title: Three released without charge after fatal arson attack in Ireland
articles.snippet: Three people - two women and one man - have been released, and one person remains in custody, gardaí say.
articles.full_text:
Three released without charge after fatal arson attack
- Published
Three people, who were arrested in connection with a suspected arson attack which killed four family members in the Republic of Ireland, have been released, gardaÃ (Irish police) have said.
Philip and Kim English and two of their children - nine-year-old Jayden and 12-year-old Callum - died after their home in Birch Avenue, on the outskirts of Waterford was set on fire earlier this month.
A man aged in his 20s and a woman in her 30s were previously charged in connection with the attack.
On Saturday, gardaÃ said three people - two women in their 30s and a man in his 50s - who were arrested on Tuesday have been released without charge.
A fourth person, a man in his 20s who was arrested on Thursday, remains in custody.

articles.title: Australian MP's condition improves after alleged car attack
articles.snippet: The independent MP is now in a serious but stable condition, according to the Melbourne hospital.
articles.full_text:
Australian MP's condition improves after alleged car attack
- Published
The condition of Helen Haines, the Australian MP hit by a car five days ago in north-east Victoria, has improved from critical to serious but stable.
The independent MP, 65, had both her legs amputated after what authorities say was a deliberate attack outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on Monday.
In the latest update on Saturday morning, the Alfred Hospital in Melbourne said Haines was in a serious but stable condition, the first improvement since she was airlifted there.
Her alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, was arrested shortly after the incident and has since appeared in court on three charges.
The politician's husband, Phil Haines, said on Wednesday that the "horrendous incident" had caused his wife significant injuries but "her heart and her mind" were "in good shape".
Nugent, who was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the MP, appeared in court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official.
Police said more charges might be laid, including attempted murder.
His lawyer said his client had "mental health concerns" but did not give any further detail.
Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.
Investigators are looking into whether drug use or medication played a part in the incident.
Nugent's family has said they were long-time friends with Haines.
Shortly after the alleged attack, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told ABC television that there had been a "rise in temperature" and "too much shouting, not enough discourse" in Australia.
Haines, known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action, entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife.

articles.title: Do abstaining voters hold the key to Brazil’s 2026 presidential election?
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Some 21 percent of Brazilian adults did not cast a ballot in the first round of voting. Will they affect the run-off?
articles.full_text:
Sao Paulo, Brazil – The first time she voted in a Brazilian presidential election, in 2014, Larissa Campelo voted for centre-right Senator Aecio Neves. Four years later, in the next presidential race, she supported a centre-left candidate, former Sao Paulo Mayor Fernando Haddad.
But ahead of what is expected to be one of Brazil’s tightest presidential run-offs ever, the 30-year-old mother of one has decided she has had enough with politics.
She is abstaining from the vote on Sunday, just as she did during the first round of the election on October 4.
Voting is compulsory for most Brazilian adults. But Campelo is part of a historically large chunk of the electorate sitting out this year's presidential race.
Some 33.4 million Brazilian adults did not show up to vote in the first round, resulting in a 21 percent abstention rate, the highest for a general election since 1998.
“It’s my form of protest. I don’t want to dirty my hands with these candidates,” said Campelo, who lives in the Sao Paulo city of Araraquara.
“This isn’t apathy. It’s because I don’t feel there’s anyone qualified enough to earn my vote.”
But appealing to abstaining voters like Campelo may prove to be a path to victory in Sunday's run-off.
A dead heat
The final vote features two presidential candidates well known in Brazil's political establishment.
The left-wing contender, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, is the incumbent president, seeking an unprecedented fourth, non-consecutive term in office.
His rival, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, is a member of a far-right political dynasty, hoping to follow in the footsteps of his father, imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro.
In the first round of voting, Bolsonaro won 47 percent of votes cast, surpassing Lula’s 45 percent. Just 2.2 million ballots separated them, out of more than 158.7 million registered voters.
The final round is set to be even tighter. The research firm Quaest published a poll on Wednesday that showed the two candidates in a statistical deadlock.
Bolsonaro earned 50.5 percent of respondents' support, well within the margin of error for Lula's 49.5 percent.
But experts say polarisation within Brazilian politics has created a population of voters unwilling to cast a ballot for either Lula or Bolsonaro.
In the Quaest poll, 52 percent of respondents said they would never vote for Bolsonaro.
Some 47 percent said the same for Lula, although the pollster noted that the president’s rejection rate had fallen six points in a week, in a promising sign for the incumbent.
A polarised political climate
Joao Guilherme Bastos dos Santos, a director at the Democracy in Check Institute, an independent research nonprofit, explained that polarisation reinforces the public's disengagement with politics.
In a deeply divided political landscape, dos Santos pointed out that voter behaviour often changes.
Voters can become motivated by fear. In turn, they are more likely to vote in opposition to a candidate than in support of one.
"That creates profound exhaustion," dos Santos said. "The fighting seems to go nowhere."
Campelo, the mother in Sao Paulo, echoed that sense of exhaustion. Her decision to stay home during Sunday's election was motivated in part by her rejection of Brazil's deeply antagonistic political culture.
"Politics in Brazil has become like supporting a football team," she said. "Politicians do things wrong, and people keep defending them. It makes no sense."
The morning of her interview with Al Jazeera, Campelo said her husband's family broke into an argument over Lula on their WhatsApp group.
"People are adopting their own pet politicians," she quipped.
Who are the abstainers?
Abstaining voters like Campelo are a diverse group, according to experts. Their reasons for dodging the ballot box can vary dramatically.
Mayra Goulart, a political scientist at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, said that those who actively reject Lula and Bolsonaro may only be a minority of Brazil’s abstainers.
Many could be merely uninterested in politics. "Life is difficult enough that they don't have the headspace, time or resources to devote to politics," she explained.
Luciana Veiga, a political science professor at the Federal University of the State of Rio de Janeiro, also pointed out that Brazil’s abstainers are not merely a bloc of disillusioned voters waiting to be won over.
They may have practical considerations that prevent them from casting a ballot. “We cannot say that abstention is simply a political 'no' to voting," Veiga said.
Abstention, she noted, often occurs among people who move cities without transferring their voter registration, as well as those who have work or family care duties on election day.
There are also some voters in isolated areas who struggle to reach distant polling stations.
In addition, voting is optional for 16- and 17-year-olds, people aged 70 or older, and those who cannot read or write.
"Of Brazil's electorate of [158.7] million people, around 21 million are not legally required to vote," Veiga explained.
The penalty for failing to vote is often minor. Without justification for their absence, voters face a fine of up to 3.51 Brazilian reals — less than a dollar — and can have their registrations cancelled after three missed elections in a row.
Until these fines are paid, citizens are unable to obtain or renew passports and other ID documents, nor can they take part in the selection process for civil service jobs.
A final push for victory
With such a slim margin between the candidates, both campaigns are hoping to court the first-round abstainers ahead of Sunday’s showdown.
In the weeks since the first vote, Bolsonaro has promised new tax breaks to help boost the economy.
A central part of his platform is a pledge to address his father's legal predicament: Jair Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence following his conviction over a coup plot.
Lula, meanwhile, has made reducing abstention a central part of his second-round push.
After round one, his campaign has highlighted Lula's work to end Brazil’s six-day workweek and unveiled proposals for free public transport on weekends and debt relief for small-scale entrepreneurs.
Goulart said that these measures "have much more of an effect on those who are uninterested in politics than on those who reject the candidates".
The first round, however, seemed to hand Bolsonaro an advantage. Not only did he secure the largest number of votes, but many of the candidates who were eliminated were his right-wing competitors.
Some experts predict that the nearly 8 percent who voted for those candidates will migrate to Bolsonaro's camp in the final round.
Bolsonaro also has historical precedent on his side. Brazil began holding direct elections for president in 1989, after its return to democracy.
Since that time, no candidate who trailed in the first round of voting has ever won in the second round.
But Goulart warns against treating precedent as destiny. “A historical observation is not a causal relationship," she said.
She also pointed out that voters may act in unpredictable ways. Wednesday's Quaest poll suggests those who backed eliminated candidates in the first round have not uniformly flocked to Bolsonaro.
While the senator has attracted 43 percent of that support, Quaest found that 37 percent were leaning towards Lula — a more balanced redistribution than initially expected.
Quaest's results also indicate Lula may have an advantage among voters who abstained in the first round or left their ballot blank.
Forty percent of those respondents supported Lula in the poll, compared with 36 percent for Bolsonaro.
While poll numbers do not guarantee results, even modest fluctuations in voter participation could be decisive in such a narrow race, according to experts.
Veiga, the political science professor, believes some of the most crucial statistics will be voter participation rates in regions where each candidate has a strong base.
Lula has a left-wing stronghold in the northeast, while Bolsonaro boasts strong backing in the south and southeast.
"Look at whether turnout falls in either candidate's bases," Veiga said. "Any small movement makes a difference."

articles.title: Rybakina readies for title defence at Ningbo Open in final with Fernandez
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: The world number one will face Leylah Fernandez in the final after the unseeded Canadian beat Czech Marie Bouzkova.
articles.full_text:
Rybakina readies for title defence at Ningbo Open in final with Fernandez
The world number one will face Leylah Fernandez in the final after the unseeded Canadian beat Czech Marie Bouzkova.
Defending Ningbo Open champion Elena Rybakina overcame Russian sixth seed Diana Shnaider 6-3, 7-5 in the semifinal to reach another title clash and remind rivals of her threat before next month’s WTA Finals.
The world number one will face Leylah Fernandez in the final on Sunday after the unseeded Canadian beat Czech Marie Bouzkova by the same 6-3, 7-5 scoreline in the earlier semifinal at the Yinzhou International Tennis Centre in the eastern Chinese city.
Recommended Stories

- list 3 of 4Ronaldinho’s comeback with Ravenna at 46 set for next month at Forli
- list 4 of 4Chicago Bulls storm back from early deficit to beat Milwaukee Bucks in NBA
Australian and US Open champion Rybakina, who arrived for her title defence after a bruising defeat in Beijing and a foot injury that forced her out of Wuhan, showed flashes of her best form despite a few wobbles against the 13th-ranked Shnaider.
“She [Shnaider] played really well, and it’s always difficult to play against left-handers. We don’t have so many on the tour,” said Rybakina, who faces a similar test against Fernandez.
“I needed some time. The returns were not as bad, but during the rallies, to switch the pattern was a little bit of an issue for me, but I’m happy I managed to win in two sets.”
An aggressive start with powerful winners from deep helped three-time Grand Slam winner Rybakina take full control of the opening frame, which she sealed on her 11th set point after a sudden dip in form.
‘So many opportunities’
“It was an important game, and it was a long one,” added the top-seeded Rybakina.
“It was on my serve, and it was a struggle … I was playing the first balls really well, but I couldn’t close the game … so many opportunities, but I’m glad it went my way. She played some great shots and great rallies.”
The 27-year-old continued to struggle with the accuracy of her first serve in the next set, but won the crucial points and carved out a 4-3 advantage with a break, only to be broken to love in the 10th game.
Rybakina responded strongly to get her nose in front again in the next game with some big hitting, before closing out the victory with a much more assured display on serve to take her place in the final.
She will aim to further sharpen her game in Sunday’s final before turning her attention to the Pan Pacific Open in Tokyo next week and then launching her WTA Finals title defence at Indian Wells from November 8.
“It’s never easy,” Rybakina said about winning back-to-back trophies at the Ningbo Open. “Of course I’ll try to do my best. I’m going to fight and give my all tomorrow.”

articles.title: Sudan’s soaring fuel prices make getting by harder for workers
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Sudan is suffering from a cost-of-living crisis affecting millions across the country.
articles.full_text:
Sudan’s soaring fuel prices make getting by harder for workers
Sudan is suffering from a cost-of-living crisis affecting millions across the country.
Azhari Mohamed drives his minibus and eight passengers seven times a day from the Shagar neighbourhood in the Port of Sudan to the city centre and back again.
But despite the long hours – working from 6am to 9pm – fuel shortages in the city have made it difficult for the 60-year-old to make a living.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3Drone strike on Abyei market near Sudan-South Sudan border kills 150
- list 2 of 3Drone attack in disputed Sudan-South Sudan border region kills at least 153
- list 3 of 3How Sudan’s shift to drone warfare is fuelling a civilian crisis
Azhari’s minibus uses three gallons (11 litres) of petrol a day, costing him about 105,000 Sudanese pounds ($11.30 a day, according to Sudan’s parallel-market exchange rate). With fuel increasingly difficult to obtain, he now spends two days on the road and a third day queuing for fuel.
He can spend more than five hours waiting in line when he needs to fill the tank of his minibus and often finds petrol has run out before his turn comes. When that happens, he goes to the back of the queue at another petrol station hoping to fill up there.
The shortages have led to price rises with a gallon (3.8 litres) of petrol now costing 40,000 Sudanese pounds ($4.30) in Gazira State, south of Khartoum, while in Port Sudan it is 35,000 pounds ($3.80) a gallon.
“We can no longer work because of the fuel shortages. The transport fares are no longer enough to cover the cost of running the vehicle and our household expenses,” Azhari told Al Jazeera.
He says the long hours spent queueing for petrol is time he could spend earning money to support his family.
“I spend long hours of the day waiting to refuel, so I have to work extra hours at night to make up for the time I lose during the day,” he said. “My livelihood depends on what I earn each day.”
After subtracting his vehicle’s operating costs, Azhari has just 50,000 Sudanese pounds ($5.40) left a day, barely enough to cover the needs of his family, which includes his wife and daughter who is at university and needs support for her tuition fees and daily expenses.
“We just need fuel to be available so we can work,” he said. “If fuel is available, we will not face this obstacle.”
Due to the crisis, Sudan’s Transport Chambers Union, which regulates public and private transport services, this month raised intercity bus fares by 40% and minibus fares by 30%.
Aziza Ibrahim from the Umm al-Qura neighbourhood of Port Sudan, works as a cleaner to support her four children. Just getting to work by bus has become a huge financial burden for the 38-year-old, who has cut back her work days to three times a week due to the high travel costs.
Before the war, a journey from her home to the main transport station in the city centre cost 700 Sudanese pounds ($0.08) per passenger. Fares have since risen to 2,500 pounds ($0.27) on some routes, while others charge 2,000 pounds ($0.22).
“I go to work three days a week to reduce transport costs. I need 11,000 pounds ($1.18) a day for the round trip between my home and workplace,” she told Al Jazeera.
Transport costs now consume nearly half of Aziza’s monthly salary of 400,000 pounds ($43), while costly treatment for her diabetes is another financial burden.
“Sometimes I have to borrow money just to be able to go to work. I repay it at the beginning of the month when I receive my salary, which is barely enough to cover my family’s needs,” she told Al Jazeera.
According to the United Nations Development Programme, the war has pushed average incomes in Sudan back to levels last seen in the 1990s.
That is partly due to the effects of the civil war on Sudan’s oil sector. Fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and rival paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) began on April 15, 2023.
Last year, the Ministry of Energy and Petroleum estimated war-related losses at $20 billion. The World Bank has reported that attacks on the Balila oil field disrupted supplies to the Khartoum refinery, which previously met about 60% of the country’s demand for petrol and liquefied petroleum gas.
War damage has seen a sharp decrease in oil production, leaving Sudan reliant on imports amid the global fuel crisis that has pushed up prices of gas, petrol and diesel, among other commodities.
Economic analyst Sidi Ohaj said that the government requirements for petroleum importers have also contributed to the shortages. They include a stipulation that importers must deposit 200kg of gold in the Central Bank and own fuel storage facilities in order to operate in Sudan. Some importers have been unable to meet those requirements, forcing them out of the market which reduces supply.
“One of the causes of the current crisis is the government’s decision to regulate the operations of petroleum import companies,” Sidi told Al Jazeera. “Some companies did not meet the requirements, which led to their exit from the market. This reduced supply relative to demand.”
The government needs to urgently ease import procedures to increase domestic supplies, he said, with shortages affecting the wider economy.
But as the war between the United States and Iran continues to disrupt global energy markets, there is little hope the situation will improve any time soon.
“The continuation of the war [in Sudan], particularly drone attacks that threaten infrastructure across Sudan, is one of the main challenges facing the oil sector,” Sidi told Al Jazeera.
Prices have also risen due to the energy crisis, impacting the purchasing power of citizens and profits of businesses.
Ahmed al-Haj is a local trader in Omdurman market who sells skincare products, such as petroleum jelly, which he packages himself . He said high energy prices are costing almost all areas of his business.
“The raw materials for the products I sell are imported. Higher diesel and petrol prices have increased the cost of transporting a tonne of goods by 30 to 50 percent,” Ahmed told Al Jazeera.
“That increase is then reflected in the price of the products.”
When electricity cuts force him to use a fuel-powered generator for heating or packaging, the additional fuel costs add to his daily bills.
Deliveries within Omdurman, which previously cost 5,000 Sudanese pounds ($0.70) now cost between 10,000 and 12,000 pounds ($1.07 and $1.29). Reaching customers in other states has become impossible due to the high transport costs.
“Transport and distribution workers have also reduced the number of trips they make, leading to goods piling up at traders’ premises,” he added.

articles.title: Who was behind the deadly church shooting in Jordan?
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Authorities are investigating the rare attack on a Christian church; the assailants remain unidentified and at large.
articles.full_text:
Who was behind the deadly church shooting in Jordan?
Authorities are investigating the rare attack on a Christian church; the assailants remain unidentified and at large.
Security forces in Jordan are searching for three gunmen who opened fire at a church in Karak governorate on Friday, killing eight people and injuring dozens more, according to Jordan’s Ministry of Health.
King Abdullah II said those behind the attack would face the “harshest penalties”, as he offered his condolences to the victims’ families. He has ordered a review of the country’s security procedures for responding to terrorist attacks.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3At least seven killed after gunmen open fire at church in Jordan
- list 2 of 3Masked gunmen kill seven in attack on church funeral in Jordan
- list 3 of 3Jordan-Israel border becomes new hotspot for sophisticated drug trade
Authorities are calling this rare attack on a Christian place of worship an act of terror, with the perpetrators yet to be identified.
Here’s what we know about how the attack unfolded, and what was behind it.
What happened during the church shooting in Karak?
On Friday afternoon, three masked gunmen opened fire during a funeral in a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud.
Survivors said they heard an explosion just after the start of the service. Two attackers who arrived in a vehicle were joined by a third carrying a semi-automatic rifle. They entered the church and opened fire for several minutes.
One survivor, Nasser al-Burqan, a lawyer, told the Reuters news agency that one of the attackers, standing about two metres (6.5 feet) away, pointed a handgun at him and opened fire.
“When everything finally quietened down, I looked out the window behind me, and I saw two [assailants] – one was masked, the other was not; he was carrying a handgun,” said al-Burqan, a lawyer.
Later, his son, who had also been present, called him to say he had been shot in the leg and was being treated in hospital.
Tarek Ammarin, who was visiting a relative injured in the attack, now in hospital, said: “A massacre, a massacre in every sense of the word.”
Bahjat al-Rushda, mayor of Shihan village in Karak, joined a list of officials condemning what he called a “wicked” attack.
“God willing, this country will remain safe,” he said.
State news channel Al-Mamlaka reported that security forces were deployed to the church and were in pursuit of the two suspects who had arrived in a vehicle.
How many people were killed or injured?
Eight people were killed in the shooting, including seven who died at the scene and one who succumbed to her injuries hours after the attack, Jordan’s Petra news agency reported on Saturday.
Of the 40 people injured, 27 are still in hospital. The Director of Prince Ali Military Hospital in Karak said one person is in critical condition, after undergoing surgery.
Who carried out the attack?
The identity of the three attackers has not been confirmed, with government statements referring to them as “unknown assailants”.
Security camera footage of the attack has been circulating online, however. Video broadcast by Al-Mamlaka shows three people shooting outside the church and running towards its entrance.
Other footage also shows the attackers opening fire on a group of men outside the building trying to flee.
Jordan’s Interior Minister Mazin Al-Farrayeh said a group of “extremists” that have “no relationship to humanity” were responsible for the attack, though no specific groups were mentioned.
Why was the church targeted?
Prime Minister Jafar Hassan said on Friday that the attack was a by-product of terrorist ideology and “blind extremism”, but did not give specifics about the attackers.
The motive remains unclear since the attackers’ identities have yet to be revealed.
Where is Karak, and what do we know about its Christian community?
Karak governorate is about 120km (75 miles) south of Amman and is home to many from Jordan’s Christian minority, which makes up about 300,000 of the country’s population of 11.5 million people.
Taylor Luck, senior Middle East correspondent at the Christian Science Monitor, told Al Jazeera that Jordan’s Christians “pride themselves on [their] interfaith solidarity and coexistence”.
He said that Christians and Muslims have lived side-by-side in Karak for generations and that if the attack had been carried out in an attempt to divide the community, it is more likely that the “community come[s] back even stronger”.
Jordan is also home to many biblical sites that draw visitors from around the world.
What has the response been to this shooting?
Several countries, including Azerbaijan, Iraq, Poland, Palestine and Qatar, have issued statements condemning the attack and expressing their solidarity with Jordan.
Ahmed al-Tayeb, the grand imam of Al-Azhar in Cairo, a leading Sunni religious institution, offered his condolences to the families of the victims, calling the shooting a “heinous terrorist attack”.
“This crime contradicts the teachings of the Abrahamic religions and reveals that its perpetrators are devoid of all compassion, humanity and morality,” he wrote in a social media post.
The United States embassy in Jordan also released a statement on X offering condolences to victims and survivors of the attack.
“On behalf of the American people, we offer our most heartfelt condolences to the victims and survivors of the terror attack today at a church in Karak, Jordan,” it said.
The Jordanian Prime Minister declared three days of mourning following the attack, with flags to be flown at half-mast over government and public buildings.
Has Jordan experienced similar attacks before?
Yes, although they are rare.
In 2016, the ISIL (ISIS) group carried out a series of attacks across Karak, including a deadly siege on a Crusader-era castle in which 10 people were killed, including a Canadian tourist and seven police officers. Dozens of others were injured.
Four attackers were later killed by Jordanian security forces following a long standoff.

FIFA’s Infantino touts global re-election support amid resignation questions
Support from Asian federation bolsters FIFA’s Gianni Infantino as he seeks re-election as president for a fourth term.
FIFA president Gianni Infantino laughed off questions about whether he had considered resigning in the wake of the failed FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, pointing to overwhelming support from member associations around the globe.
Three months after facing calls to resign after he abandoned the proposal that sought private investment in a new entity controlling commercial rights linked to major FIFA competitions, Infantino now finds himself in a position of strength.
Recommended Stories

- list 3 of 4Ronaldinho’s comeback with Ravenna at 46 set for next month at Forli

His prospects for re-election strengthened on Friday after the head of Asian football endorsed him for a fourth term, with Asian Football Confederation (AFC) President Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa saying Asia was united behind Infantino.
“I was elected by 211 member associations from all over the world. I think what is important is that in an organisation like FIFA, there can be different views, different points of view,” Infantino told the BBC as he laughed off a question about whether he had considered stepping down.
“But if we are serious about democracy, about the democratic process, about believing that everyone has the same vote and the same voice all over the world, that football belongs to everyone … then we need to respect as well the views of the vast, vast majority.
“I’m just coming back off Tokyo where the Asian Football Confederation has fully endorsed me. I was in Cape Verde where all African countries have endorsed me. I’m speaking to all associations everywhere in the world.”
The AFC had previously joined European body UEFA and CONCACAF, which represents North and Central America and the Caribbean, in criticising the FFE proposal.
But a divided CONCACAF and the AFC’s U-turn have left Europe increasingly isolated while exposing the lack of a viable alternative candidate for the FIFA presidency.
Infantino is seeking a fourth term until 2031, and potential candidates must submit their nominations by November 18.
He apologised at a FIFA Council meeting in Zurich last week for the way the FFE proposal was handled, but that did not sway European football associations, such as Germany and England.
However, the 56-year-old Swiss-Italian administrator added: “It’s OK to disagree … but then we need to be able to move on.
“There are different points of view. It’s not always easy to bring them all under one roof, but we need to respect, and I do respect all opinions all views,” Infantino added.
“Then, it will be up to the FIFA member associations to decide who they want as a president and how they want FIFA to be run.”

articles.title: Iran says won’t allow US warships to get close as Trump ponders new attacks
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera

articles.full_text:
Iran says won’t allow US warships to get close as Trump ponders new attacks
Iranian officials, media and analysts sense war is closer, but signal there will be no backing down.
Tehran, Iran – Iran’s armed forces say they are prepared to fire on United States warships as President Donald Trump said Washington was still deliberating new attacks or continued pressure on Iran.
Trump told supporters at a rally in Florida on Friday that the US military “may do another Epic Fury”, in reference to the extensive bombing campaign against Iran at the start of the war. He had earlier questioned whether to end the conflict quickly through huge attacks on Iran or let pressure on Tehran from a naval blockade and sanctions persist.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3Lebanese sceptical Israeli polls will bring change, end occupation of south
- list 2 of 3Keeping the world safe when no one is in charge
- list 3 of 3Why is Israel launching a new military operation in the occupied West Bank?
But Ali Abdollahi, chief of general staff of the Iranian armed forces, asserted that the US Navy is incapable of re-entering Iran’s territorial waters or its periphery due to Iran’s ability to target any vessel in the region.
“The US president can only dream of their soldiers and military again entering the Persian Gulf. They will take this wish to the grave for good,” he said in a statement carried by state media on Saturday morning.
Abdollahi also said US rhetoric about the war pointed to a basic contradiction: US claims that Iran’s military capabilities have been mostly destroyed during the war were nullified by its refusal to bring its aircraft carriers and support vessels closer to Iranian territory.
He added that Iranian forces were determined to “drown” the US and Israel in a “quagmire” in retaliation for their surprise attack on Iran on February 28, starting an eight-month war and plunging the whole region into instability.
Strait of Hormuz
Vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz continue to be attacked by Iran. Together with the increased odds of renewed war, this has driven up oil prices and sent Brent crude to its highest price since April, at about $117.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said seven tankers were attacked or hit mines overnight into Thursday. It then claimed on Friday that two supertankers struck mines. The IRGC has said its military doctrine is now more offensive, and Washington has reportedly ordered many diplomatic personnel to leave Saudi Arabia, with others set to depart other countries in the region.
The Iran-allied Houthis in Yemen also continued to exchange attacks with Saudi Arabia, hitting Riyadh again on Saturday, with the international airport in Dammam and the Shaybah oilfield targeted in recent days. Saudi forces have bombed Marib, Taiz and several other Yemeni provinces under Houthi control.
In southern Lebanon, Friday brought further reported Israeli air attacks around Nabatieh and artillery fire near Zawtar ash-Sharqiyah. Iran has linked this front to its war with the US and Israel, in the past demanding that any ceasefire with Washington also cover Lebanon.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, facing an election on October 27 which comes days before the November 3 mid-term elections in the US, also ordered a lockdown of the occupied West Bank after a Palestinian attack killed two soldiers in Hebron. The Houthis have also launched attacks on Israel linked to events in Gaza and the West Bank, highlighting how wider regional peace now depends on events in multiple theatres, including Lebanon, the occupied West Bank and Gaza.
Netanyahu has reiterated his desire to overthrow the Iranian government, leading several state-linked media and analysts in Iran to claim that Tehran has activated a “dead hand” doctrine. That allegedly enables military attacks against US, Israeli and regional interests to continue from across the country’s 31 provinces if senior Iranian figures are again assassinated as at the start of the war.
The IRGC has threatened seabed internet and communication cables if Iran’s civilian infrastructure is again targeted by the US and Israel. US-based Axios on Saturday cited US intelligence claiming that Iranian authorities had “substantially increased” efforts to strike American officials in the Middle East and beyond.
Diplomacy in Istanbul
Mediated negotiations between Iran and the US are no closer to yielding results. But regional and European powers held a coordination meeting in Istanbul on Friday and announced their expectations for the future of the war.
Top diplomats from Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt met with the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Italy, with neither the US nor Iran participating.
“We agree that a new attack on Iran would widen the war and spread the conflict across the region,” Turkiye’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said after the meeting. “Military intervention in Iran is by no means a solution. No one is endorsing it at this point.”
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said his government held Iran and the Houthis responsible for instability in the Middle East.
But the foreign ministers of the four regional countries issued a joint statement that said “Israeli occupation was the main source of instability in the region and beyond.”
In line with resolving the US-Israel war on Iran, the four regional countries supported the Islamabad memorandum of understanding signed in June and a negotiated settlement, while demanding unrestricted passage through the Strait of Hormuz. The group said they opposed attacks on civilians and commercial vessels, and condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and its Red Sea shipping interests.
The Istanbul meeting once again displayed a “gap between diplomatic claims and realities in the field”, Nour News, an outlet affiliated with Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, argued in an analysis on Saturday.
It said the US and European powers – not Iran – must make concessions first. The outlet presented reopening the Strait of Hormuz as conditional on the US accepting Tehran’s demands and acknowledging responsibility for attacking Iran and Yemen.
Most Iranian newspapers on Saturday focused on signs of war, including rising oil prices.
The headline from hardline Vatan-e Emrooz reported that the price of a barrel of Brent crude rising above $117 was “evidence of disgrace for Trump”. Reformist Etemad said US and Israeli actions were signalling that the “zero hour” of another intense round of the war was approaching.
Reza Nasri, a Tehran-based foreign policy analyst with links to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said that after being subject to decades of attacks, nuclear sabotage, sanctions and violated deals by the US, Iran’s strategy was now “enough is enough.
“Iran has reached its verdict. It will no longer negotiate under bombardment, honour agreements the other side treats as optional, or accept the killing of its children and the penury of its people as routine instruments of policy,” he wrote on X. “It will put an end to this cycle, and it will do so by all necessary means”.

articles.title: US military needs ‘urgent revolutionary institutional change’ to prepare for modern war, Petraeus says
articles.snippet: Ret. Army Gen. David Petraeus praised the Pentagon’s new Autonomous Warfare Command but said the U.S. must rapidly prepare for modern autonomous war.
articles.full_text:
Unmanned systems now inflict more than 90% of Russia’s casualties on the front lines in Ukraine, yet no NATO military, including America’s, has begun the overhaul that kind of war demands, Ret. Army Gen. David Petraeus said Oct. 16, weeks after the Pentagon announced a new command for autonomous warfare.
The extent of the drone war is underestimated, with Ukraine and Russia each using roughly 10,000 drones a day, the former CIA director and onetime commander of U.S. Central Command said, speaking at an American Primary Aluminum Association event in Washington.
“This is an unmanned systems war,” Petraeus said. “Tanks aren’t survivable there anymore.”
For Ukraine, drones and unmanned weapons have become central to how the country has leveraged a smaller, outgunned force against a much larger, better-financed adversary for almost five years.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy ordered the creation of a new Unmanned Systems Forces military branch in 2024, and the Defense Ministry has said time and again that developing more autonomous weapons is a top priority.
But for the rest of the world, Petraeus said, the fighting in Ukraine is a window into the future and a warning about the dangers of being underprepared for the battles to come.
“Really, no NATO country and not even the United States is undertaking yet the urgent revolutionary institutional change that should be taken based on what we see in Ukraine, which is the future of war,” he said.
The U.S. needs a new concept of warfare that runs through force structure, training, procurement, personnel policy and bases, the general said, replacing much of the legacy, heavily manned equipment with unmanned systems that are cheaper and far more numerous.
“What’s going to happen is we’ll see the introduction of autonomous systems really for the first time in warfare,” Petraeus said.
Washington is making “some commendable steps” toward developing these weapons, according to Petraeus, including establishing a new Autonomous Warfare Command that requires each military branch to stand up its own component command.
“But my hope is that they will not just create an unmanned systems force in terms of force structure, but that they will also spur the initiation of true institutional change,” Petraeus said.
That includes how the U.S. buys weapons, Petraeus said, calling for “very, very substantial manufacturing capacity but not necessarily producing all the time.”
“You want it to be able to make software changes every week, hardware changes every few weeks, which is what’s going on in Ukraine because the enemy continues to evolve and Russia’s been innovating very substantially as well,” he said.
Ukraine will produce as many as 20 million unmanned systems this year, Zelenskyy said in a July speech, with a shortage of trained operators and the acquisition of some weapons components — including optics, gimbals, brushless motors and fiber-optic cable — becoming the domestic industry’s production bottleneck.
The general also rejected the idea that the U.S. war with Iran has hurt Washington’s ability to help Kyiv, though he acknowledged the U.S. has used “a fair number of missile interceptors,” which “makes it more difficult to share those with others around the world.”
The war has consumed between one-half and two-thirds of the U.S. inventory of certain missile-defense interceptors, according to a Congressional Budget Office estimate released in September.
“We can help the Ukrainians in any way in which we decide to assist them,” Petraeus said. “These are policy decisions.”

articles.title: ‘The West can’t stop me’: Space wars heat up as Russia tails a Ukraine-linked US satellite
articles.snippet: Washington blamed Moscow for deliberately moving a Russian military satellite with an undisclosed mission close last week to a U.S.-registered satellite.
articles.full_text:
KYIV, Ukraine — Washington blamed Moscow at the United Nations on Wednesday for deliberately moving a Russian military satellite with an undisclosed mission “dangerously” close last week to a U.S.-registered satellite believed to serve Ukraine, with officials vowing to defend American interests in space.
The Russian satellite, Cosmos 2612, spent more than two weeks maneuvering toward ICEYE-X36, a radar satellite operated by the American arm of Finnish company ICEYE that supplies imagery to Ukraine’s military through some of its spacecraft, then shadowed it from as close as a third of a mile through the weekend of Oct. 17.
U.S. Undersecretary of State Thomas G. DiNanno called the Russian satellite’s behavior “threatening,” and said the country had been “intentionally maneuvering dangerously close to a commercial satellite, behaviors consistent with on-orbit weapons operations.”
Space historian and former NASA astrophysicist Jonathan McDowell said that he believed it is the first rendezvous in low Earth orbit between two active satellites without one owner’s approval.
The close encounter came weeks after Air Force Secretary Troy Meink publicly confirmed that the U.S. has weapons in orbit and the Space Force picked two companies to build space-to-space reconnaissance satellites. It also followed reports that trillionaire Elon Musk — under White House orders — slowed the military-grade Starlink that Ukraine relies on, rendering some of the country’s essential air defense weapons useless.
The operation fits a wider Russian campaign of intimidation against Europe and the U.S. that lets Russian President Vladimir Putin “poke the West in the eye and watch the West do nothing,” according to Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
“They prove a point – the West can’t stop me,” Swope added Wednesday during a CSIS panel on the encounter.
As the U.S. and its allies increasingly rely on commercial capabilities for national security, key assets like satellites have “become vulnerabilities that can be exploited by our adversary,” according to Greg Gillinger, senior vice president of strategy and development at Virginia-based Integrity ISR, who also spoke on the CSIS panel.
The impact of a possible satellite attack could reach well beyond one company or country, since commercial satellites now carry much of the imagery and connectivity militaries fight with, experts said. Musk’s Starlink slowdown in Ukraine showed how quickly a military force can suffer when that access is throttled without notice — and how easily local geopolitical conflicts can explode into global security crises.
On Oct. 12, commercial trackers feeding the U.S. military’s Joint Commercial Operations cell flagged the possible rendezvous when Cosmos 2612 slid into ICEYE-X36’s orbit roughly 345 miles above Earth, according to Integrity ISR’s newsletter.
On Oct. 15 and 16, the Russian satellite moved from more than 200 miles behind ICEYE-X36 to roughly 3 miles away before moving in closer and holding position through the weekend, tracking firm LeoLabs said in a statement reported by CNN.
Both satellites travel at roughly 4 miles (7 kilometers) per second, so getting two objects “within a hundred meters or even a kilometer” of each other is “the equivalent of flying in a very tight formation in an aircraft,” Gillinger said.
“Russia didn’t accidentally get within a kilometer of X36,” he said. “It is an indication of intent that they’re sending a message.”
ICEYE, whose radar satellites see through clouds, smoke and darkness, expanded cooperation with Ukraine’s military, pledging continued imagery “on tactical timelines,” according to a January statement. However, the company has not confirmed which of its satellites serve Kyiv.
Moscow has warned since the first year of its full-scale invasion that Western commercial satellites helping Ukraine could become legitimate military targets.
ICEYE said it is “aware of the situation and tracking it closely” and that its “constellation architecture is designed for continuity and resilience,” a spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine earlier this week.
Russia’s intent behind the satellite maneuvers remains unclear. According to LeoLabs, an American space technology company, possible aims range from intelligence collection and close inspection to coercion and groundwork for future operations against satellites.
The maneuvers demonstrated capabilities that could be used to “inspect, characterize, shadow, or potentially interfere with another spacecraft,” though they “do not establish hostile intent,” the company said.
Analysts could not yet say whether Moscow planned an attack and then reversed course, or was orbiting nearby for another purpose entirely.
Russia could have been doing “a dry run” for a future attack, or the satellite could have been carrying a weapon, from a jammer to a laser to a projectile, Swope explained.
“Was the intent to blow up the satellite? No,” he said. “Was the intent to put some type of energy on the satellite? Probably… I don’t know why you’d need to maneuver in this way, this close, unless you wanted to do something that involved putting energy on that satellite.”
The Russian satellite has since pulled back, but not far.
It was again flying at ICEYE-X36’s altitude on Wednesday, holding roughly 250 miles (400 kilometers) behind it, and could “easily close that gap again at the time and place of their choosing,” Gillinger said.
Russia could try to approach another ICEYE satellite within weeks, as two more satellites from the same launch will soon line up with the orbit of a second satellite, ICEYE-X37, according to Integrity ISR.
If they move in, “we could see another scenario where another commercial satellite is closely trailed by one of these Russian satellites,” Gillinger said.
The retreat began Oct. 18, two days after President Donald Trump signed an executive order waiving tariffs and most economic restrictions on Russia.
Swope said Trump’s move to ease sanctions “could have been a reason why Putin said, ‘You know, now’s not the time to exacerbate tensions specifically with the United States. Maybe we should pause this operation.’”
“If you’re getting close to a deal on something, why jeopardize that?” he said.
The potential for a conflict in space has been growing in recent months.
Washington “appears to lack response options” if Russia threatened U.S. military and commercial satellites with a nuclear weapon in orbit, according to the conclusions from a 2025 war-game scenario where fictional Russian space objects threatened American interests.
There is no public indication that Cosmos 2612 carries a nuclear weapon, but Swope said that there is also still no internationally recognized rule for determining if a maneuver like this one should be considered hostile — or what international standards should be followed in a response.
“Even though we all can make a good case on why this was [hostile], there’s no norm that you could point to,” he said.
Without a clear response plan or real consequences for aggression, menacing satellite moves like this one are “literally just a spigot that Russia could turn on and off” to increase pressure on adversaries, Swope said.
Russia, he added, “is going to turn it on again.”
